extracted.intended_audience: judge advocates, military legal officers, quartermasters, and Army administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Legal and administrative standards governing government agencies and instrumentalities in the U.S. military (post exchanges, company funds, laundries, custody of funds, and related officer responsibilities). Covers creation, recognition, permissible practices, duties, liability for losses, and procedural reporting rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrest and delivery of soldier during military occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: The arrest and delivery of a soldier serving in the Philippine Islands or Cuba to U.S. authorities is not, during military occupation, a matter of international extradition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a soldier so serving has been indicted in one of the States, the War Department may legally direct his surrender to such civil officer as may be sent, supplied with the proper papers, to receive him. (Citations: C. 0900, 6055, Mar. 1899; 8825, June 15, 1900; 13289, Nov. 12, 1902.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Flag recognition under statutes and regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The U.S. flag is described in the Revised Statutes; flags of foreign nations and the Geneva Convention flag are recognized under international law and Army Regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except for flag of truce and certain guidons distinguishing military persons/units, this office has no knowledge of other flags being officially recognized by War Department or United States in ordinary sense. (O. 22135, Sept. 26, 1907.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-mark cannot comprise national or state insignia
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act of February 20, 1905, a trade-mark cannot be registered which consists of or comprises the flag, coat of arms, or other insignia of the United States, or any simulation thereof, or of any State or municipality, or of any foreign nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: (Cited holdings: a. 499, May 6, 1905, and Sept. 28, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: State may prohibit improper uses of the flag
rubrics_metrics.description: It is within the authority of a State to prohibit the flag from being put to improper uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held in cited decisions; several States have statutes to enforce respect for the flag. (C. 499, Mar. 18, 1907 and Apr. 12, 1907; see Halter v. Nebraska, 205 U.S. 34.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Insult to flag and public peace remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: If the U.S. flag is insulted in such a manner as to constitute a menace to the public peace, state law should be invoked to provide an adequate remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where insult rises to menace to public peace, the law of the State can be used; see cited decision (G. 599, Feb. 21, 1906).

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Department cannot accept flags absent legislation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Executive Department has no authority in the absence of legislation to accept any flag on behalf of the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recaptured flags may be returned to a regiment if still in the service, but formal acceptance by Executive requires statute. (C. 10004, Mar. 19, 1901; P. 118, Feb. 21, 1893.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Creation and recognition of government agencies/instrumentalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Government agencies and instrumentalities (e.g., post exchanges, laundries, company funds) may be created by legislative or executive authority and are recognized as such for purposes of administration and appropriations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress may establish agencies it deems necessary for efficiency/comfort of troops; Secretary of War may authorize establishment (e.g., post laundries) and prescribe regulations for administration. Practice has existed for over a century. (C. 18224, Sept. 8, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Post exchanges are government instrumentalities (not corporations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Post exchanges are government agencies/instrumentalities recognized by acts of Congress; they are not corporations but operate as cooperative stores for the post.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because they are government instrumentalities, their funds are quasi-public and protected; historical Treasury and War Department holdings confirmed non-taxable status and allowed certain collection/stoppage practices. (See discussion pages 642–647.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Stoppage of pay to reimburse government agency losses
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoppages of pay may legally be made to reimburse the post-exchange fund or other government instrumentality for losses for which officers or enlisted men are responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The pay of officers and enlisted men, whether active or retired, may be stopped to reimburse post-exchange, company, hospital, or regimental funds. In the estate of deceased, amounts due the exchange may be deducted from pay and allowances due the estate. (C. 3171, June 7, 1897; multiple citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Status of pay turned over to company commander
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay turned over to a company commander at payment continues to be government funds until the soldier performs an act that operates as a technical reduction to possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the soldier requests the commander to pay creditors, that portion is treated as reduced to possession. Where a well-established custom exists to collect at the pay table, that custom may be regarded as a soldier's request and such amounts are technically reduced to possession and payable to creditors immediately; remaining balance retains character of public funds and should be returned to the paymaster. (O. 12227, Feb. 12, 1907; Oct. 12, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-public character of post/company/hospital funds and standard of care
rubrics_metrics.description: Post exchange, company, hospital, bakery funds are quasi-public funds; officers in charge are officials charged with custody of public funds and owe a greater degree of care than gratuitous bailees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability is that of an official performing a duty with a material trust; loss due to lack of proper care can render the officer liable. Numerous case illustrations provided (e.g., unsecured package loss; failure to seal sack; secure, bolted steel box not negligence). (C. 13597; C. 19112; G. 20003; C. 25552.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of culpable handling of funds (when officer held responsible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Officer held responsible when funds were handled without proper precautions: unsecured package placed in blouse and lost; large sum in unsealed sack delivered to enlisted man and stage company resulting in shortage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where officer did not use due care in conveying funds (not sealing/stamping, placing in insecure place, entrusting to unsuitable carrier), held liable for losses. (P. 511, June 7, 1892; C. 19112, Feb. 2, 1906.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of non-culpable handling of funds (when officer not held responsible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Officer not held responsible when the funds were kept in reasonably secure manner (e.g., steel box bolted to floor) or where entrusting funds to apparently reliable noncommissioned officer in urgent business was reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of a securely bolted steel box, or reasonable trust in a reliable NCO when circumstances require it, may relieve officer of liability. (C. 25552; O. 16065, Mar. 24, 1904; C. 29057, Oct. 3, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation of deposit duties and resulting liability
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer who, instead of personally attending to bank deposit, sends a subordinate (e.g., steward) who appropriates funds is liable for the loss as having failed to take proper care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Officer must exercise required degree of care and not delegate critical duties imprudently; sending a steward to deposit and resulting embezzlement or abscondment held officer responsible. (P. 64, 138, Mar. 8, 1894; C. 13867, Jan. 2, 1903.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility for day’s receipts and steward turnover rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Under paragraph 337 (Army Regulations), the officer in charge is not responsible for the day's receipts until turned over to him by the steward the following morning, absent evidence of negligence or want of precaution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If officer followed regulations and there is no negligence, loss of that day's receipts may not be charged to him. Case example: post exchange robbed of part day's receipts and small change left with steward. (P. 58, 437, Mar. 28, 1893.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation and reporting of losses (post council procedure)
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of loss of regimental, bakery, exchange, company, or mess funds, circumstances will be investigated and reported by the post council with recommendation as to responsibility for decision of the department commander.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where post is outside department command (e.g., Alcatraz Island), report forwarded by post commander to the Adjutant General of the Army. (Paragraph 318; C. 24380, Feb. 6, 1909.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Company fund debts and permitted expenditures
rubrics_metrics.description: Debts from officers to a company on account of boarding are debts to the company fund; expenditure from company fund must be solely for the benefit of the company; company fund is not liable for debts of an unauthorized company exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: no authority to loan company fund to enlisted men to enable athletic representation; expense of bond to secure bank against loss on lost certificate may be paid from company fund. (Paragraph 331; pages cited.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Soldier laundering payments requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier cannot be required to pay for the laundering of his clothes by an exchange or company laundry unless his clothes were actually laundered there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirms limits on what an exchange may charge a soldier; related appropriations and regulations for post laundries noted. (See IV on page 650–651; G.O. references.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers of government agencies not subject to interference
rubrics_metrics.description: The powers of a government agency as established by Congress cannot be interfered with by the Executive or by another government agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress-established powers for instrumentalities must be respected by other branches; doctrine illustrated in discussion of government agencies' autonomy. (See XI in synopsis.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Post exchange business limitations and officer protections
rubrics_metrics.description: Post exchanges cannot accept deposits from soldiers and cannot collect certain taxes (e.g., dog taxes); the officer in charge may represent the exchange in litigation and, if litigation is necessary, may properly request government counsel; he is not personally responsible to a creditor of the post exchange merely because regulations make him responsible for management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists practical limitations on post exchange business and protections/privileges for officers in charge (allowance for services, representation, requests for counsel). (Sections II.A–D and II.B.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Membership rules for post exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations comprising the membership of a post exchange are construed as continuing organizations regardless of personnel changes; disputes as to admission of new organization resolved by department commander except in case of fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes rules on distribution where membership reduced after buying into exchange and that membership is not obligatory on units forming garrison. (Section I. Membership; pages 646–647.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Post exchange administrative miscellany (transfer, accounts, property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Government property may be transferred by a Government bureau to the post exchange; exchange may be ordered to readjust accounts with a paymaster; various administrative actions (telegrams, donations to volunteer bands, fuel charges) governed by regulations and appropriations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: post exchange may transfer funds to paymaster, contribute to volunteer band (but volunteer band not entitled to net profits), fuel & lights proper charge against Army appropriation, paragraph references provided. Fraud by steward is a military offense. (Section II.J.)
